paragraphs.heading: A century of upheaval
paragraphs.text: The Age of Revolution runs from the late 1700s to the middle of the 1800s. In that time, many major revolutionary movements broke out across most of Europe and the Americas. The era is remembered for kings with unchecked power giving way to representative governments bound by written constitutions. It also saw nation states take shape.

paragraphs.heading: Where the name comes from
paragraphs.text: The label was made popular by the British historian Eric Hobsbawm. He used it in his 1962 book The Age of Revolution: Europe 1789–1848. Revolutions in this period struck the United States, the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, France, Haiti, Ireland and Spanish America, with smaller upheavals in Switzerland, Russia and Brazil. The rebels in these places knew about one another, and to some extent they took inspiration from or copied each other.

paragraphs.heading: From America to France
paragraphs.text: Shaped by the new thinking of the Enlightenment, the American Revolution of 1765–1783 is usually treated as the opening event. France, the Netherlands and Spain helped the new United States win its independence from Britain. The French Revolution followed in 1789, and its wars carried it quickly across Europe. After Napoleon seized power in 1799, he conquered most of the continent and brought ideas such as equality before the law and a civil code, but his harsh occupation sparked national revolts, notably in Spain and Germany.

paragraphs.heading: The Americas break free
paragraphs.text: Haiti's revolution broke out in the 1790s and lasted until 1804. Spain came out of the Napoleonic Wars badly weakened and could no longer hold its American colonies. Almost all of them declared independence between 1810 and 1820, and Colombia was among the first South American nations to do so. With Spain caught up in European wars, its mainland colonies won their independence around 1820.

paragraphs.heading: Waves across Europe
paragraphs.text: Once Napoleon was beaten, the great powers of Europe met at the Congress of Vienna in 1814–15 and forged the Holy Alliance, hoping to stop future revolutions, and they put the old monarchies back. Even so, revolt returned to southern Europe in 1820, in Portugal, Spain, Italy and Greece. Two more similar waves shook the continent, in 1830 and in 1848, also known as the Spring of Nations. Demands for democracy often blended with drives for independence or national unity, as in Italy, Germany, Poland and Hungary, and the violent crushing of the Spring of Nations closed the era.

paragraphs.heading: What the revolutions left
paragraphs.text: Seen over the long run, the revolutions mostly succeeded. They spread far and wide the ideals of liberalism and republicanism, along with the idea of overthrowing aristocracies, kings and state churches. Their success showed that a revolution in the modern sense, setting up a radically new government through a popular uprising, could actually work. Revolutionary movements and ideas have existed ever since.

paragraphs.heading: Burke's two verdicts
paragraphs.text: The writings of Edmund Burke weaken the picture of one shared Atlantic story. In 1774 he backed the American colonists, arguing that the crown was taking their property and rights without consent. In 1790 he condemned the French Revolution, because there the revolutionaries themselves were stripping away property, customary and religious rights. In both cases he followed Montesquieu's view that owning property is a core part of personal freedom.
